Shelomith
she-lō'mith
n. (a name borne by both men and women in Scripture: the Danite mother of the blasphemer, an Izharite chief, a keeper of the dedicated treasures, and a daughter of Zerubbabel)
From Hebrew Shelomith, from shalom, peace — “peaceful”. The irony of the first bearer's appearance in Leviticus is not lost on the reader; the name means peace and the episode is a stoning.

Biblical Definition

Shelomith is one of the few names in Scripture borne by both men and women. The first is a woman of Dan, named in a passage nobody forgets: her son, whose father was an Egyptian, strove with a man of Israel in the camp and “blasphemed the name of the LORD, and cursed. And they brought him unto Moses: (and his mother's name was Shelomith, the daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan)” (Lev 24:11). The man was put in ward until the mind of the LORD should be shown, and the law given there governs the case for ever — and applies alike to the stranger and to the homeborn (Lev 24:16). The other bearers are Levites and royalty. “Of the sons of Izhar; Shelomith the chief” (1Ch 23:18) heads an Izharite house in David's courses. Another, of the line of Eliezer, held one of the great trusts of the kingdom: he “and his brethren were over all the treasures of the dedicated things, which David the king, and the chief fathers, the captains over thousands and hundreds, and the captains of the host, had dedicated” (1Ch 26:26) — the spoils of the wars, given to God. And a Shelomith is the sister of Meshullam and Hananiah, a daughter of Zerubbabel, named in the royal genealogy after the exile (1Ch 3:19).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Shelomith; in sacred history it is the name of several persons, men and women, from a Danite mother in the wilderness to a daughter of Zerubbabel.

SHELOMITH, n. The name signifies peaceful, from the word for peace.

A woman of the tribe of Dan, the daughter of Dibri, whose son blasphemed the name of the LORD.

A chief of the sons of Izhar, in the courses of the Levites under David.

A Levite of the line of Eliezer, set over the treasures of the dedicated things.

A daughter of Zerubbabel, named with her brethren in the genealogy of the house of David.

Key Scripture

Lev 24:11 — "And the Israelitish woman's son blasphemed the name of the LORD, and cursed. And they brought him unto Moses: (and his mother's name was Shelomith, the daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan:)"

Lev 24:16 — "And he that blasphemeth the name of the LORD, he shall surely be put to death, and all the congregation shall certainly stone him: as well the stranger, as he that is born in the land, when he blasphemeth the name of the LORD, shall be put to death."

1Ch 23:18 — "Of the sons of Izhar; Shelomith the chief."

1Ch 26:26 — "Which Shelomith and his brethren were over all the treasures of the dedicated things, which David the king, and the chief fathers, the captains over thousands and hundreds, and the captains of the host, had dedicated."

Modern Corruption

Blasphemy is now treated as a victimless offence against a fiction, and the third commandment as a rule about crude language; Scripture treats the name of God as the most serious thing a man can handle.

expand to see more

The blasphemy case in Leviticus 24 is the passage modern readers most want to explain away, and the explanations usually rest on the assumption that no real injury is done when a name is cursed. The Bible's premise is the opposite: God is, His name is Himself made known, and to curse it is the nearest a creature comes to striking at his Maker. The dictionary does not hold that the civil penalty of the Mosaic judicial law binds the modern state; those judicial laws expired with the nation to which they were given, their general equity only remaining. It does hold that the offence is exactly as grave as Leviticus says it is, and that the third commandment is not chiefly about coarse speech. “Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain” (Exo 20:7) — the commandment with a threat attached to it.

Two further things in the passage are worth naming because they cut against modern assumptions in both directions. First, the law is applied without partiality: “as well the stranger, as he that is born in the land”. The son of an Egyptian father received exactly the justice an Israelite would have received, neither harsher nor lighter, which is the biblical rule for courts — ye shall not respect persons in judgment. Second, the mother is named and her tribe given, and the record then leaves her alone. Scripture does not sentence Shelomith for her son's sin; the man who blasphemed bore his own iniquity, as Ezekiel would later insist at length: “The soul that sinneth, it shall die” (Eze 18:20).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Shelomith (H8019), Shelomith, peaceful; shalom (H7965), peace; naqab (H5344), to pierce, to blaspheme by pronouncing; qalal (H7043), to curse, make light of; qodesh (H6944), dedicated, holy.

expand to see more

Hebrew Shelomith (H8019) — Shelomith; peaceful, from the word for peace.

Hebrew shalom (H7965) — peace, wholeness, welfare; the root of the name.

Hebrew naqab (H5344) — to pierce, to specify, to blaspheme; the verb of Lev 24:11.

Hebrew qalal (H7043) — to be light, to curse, to treat with contempt; joined with it there.

Hebrew qodesh (H6944) — holiness, a dedicated thing; the treasures the Levite Shelomith kept.

Usage

"“His mother's name was Shelomith, the daughter of Dibri” — a name preserved in the hardest chapter."

"“As well the stranger, as he that is born in the land” — one law, no partiality."

"“Over all the treasures of the dedicated things” — the spoils of war, given to God and kept by a Levite."
